summary:
Lower Silesian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, and the inventory records no local deviation in law or enforcement that would distinguish this voivodeship from the country as a whole. A trans visitor in Wrocław or anywhere else in the province meets the Polish national position on custody, entry and documents.

Detention is the clearest documented risk. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention published the case of a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, whom a Polish regional court placed in a guarded centre for male foreigners. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten a person's life or health, and wherever the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that statutory bar, and she was freed only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander; the page was updated on 28 March 2024.

The March 2024 case sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention, and therefore bears directly on any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship. The statutory protection existed in writing and did not operate until a third party invoked it.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate.

The same judgment left the alleged breaches of Article 3 and Article 14 undecided. It binds Poland and governs healthcare for trans people in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, Lower Silesian among them, though placement decisions in custody remain individual and unpredictable in practice.
tangentialFactors:
Two distinct custodial settings are documented, not one. The March 2024 case concerns immigration detention for foreign nationals in a guarded centre; the July 2024 judgment concerns a person serving a prison sentence. A short-term trans visitor is exposed chiefly to the first of these, where placement is decided by the Border Guard rather than by a prison governor.

The release in the March 2024 case followed an application by the Association for Legal Intervention to the Border Guard Post commander, not a court order. The bar on placing a person in a facility where life or health would be threatened was already in force, and it took NGO pressure to make it bite.

The European Court of Human Rights declined to decide the Article 3 and Article 14 claims, so no binding finding yet establishes that Polish custody conditions or differential treatment breach those provisions for trans detainees. Medication denial, by contrast, is now litigable and has been won.
localsOnly:
For trans people held in Polish prisons, the European Court of Human Rights judgment of 11 July 2024 establishes that hormone-replacement therapy cannot simply be withheld: the refusal in Siedlce prison was found to have no reasonable legal grounds and to be disproportionate, with EUR 8,000 awarded in damages. The ruling binds Poland and applies across all voivodeships.

The statutory bar on placement in facilities where a person's life or health would be threatened, or where signs of violence are present, protects residents as well as foreign nationals in guarded centres. The March 2024 case shows that the protection is enforced only when someone raises it on the detained person's behalf.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a Lower Silesian detention centre, court practice, or police practice specific to this voivodeship. Both documented cases arose elsewhere in Poland and are carried here for the national framework they establish; whether enforcement differs locally is unresolved.

The inventory does not show whether the release in March 2024 produced any change in Border Guard practice at guarded centres for male foreigners. The source records only the release following the association's application.

The Article 3 and Article 14 claims remain undecided by the European Court of Human Rights, and no Polish domestic ruling on medication denial in custody at the time of travel is recorded here.

Rules on legal document markers, entry screening, facilities access, and healthcare outside custody for trans visitors are not covered by this inventory and are unsourced for this voivodeship.
